overview.description: Tien Gow (Heaven Nine) is the oldest and most prestigious Chinese domino game. It is a trick-taking game played with a single set of 32 Chinese domino tiles. Players lead tricks with single tiles, pairs, triples, or quadruplets, and others must follow with higher-ranking tiles of the same group (Civil or Military). It is a game of deep tactical complexity and cultural heritage.

history.origins: Tien Gow dates back to the Song Dynasty and is the ancestor of many modern tile and card games. It uses the standard 32-tile Chinese domino set, which represents all possible outcomes of two six-sided dice.
timeline: 960–1279 AD: Early forms of domino games emerge in Song China.
18th Century: Tien Gow reaches its modern form and becomes favored by the elite.
19th-20th Century: Remains a popular gambling and social game in Hong Kong, Macau, and Southern China.
Present Day: Still played in traditional communities, often associated with high-stakes play and deep strategy.
history.evolution: The game's ranking system (Civil and Military suits) heavily influenced later games like Mahjong. The concept of 'Heaven' (6-6) and 'Nine' (3-6/4-5) as top ranks persists across many Chinese gambling games.
history.cultural: Used as a tool for social bonding and intellectual challenge. In traditional settings, the tiles are handled with specific etiquette and flourished during play.

setup.players: 4 players, each playing for themselves (no partnerships).
setup.deck: Full set of 32 Chinese dominoes. No wild cards.
setup.equipment: 32 tiles (traditionally wood or bone), 4 dice (to determine dealer/seat), and score markers.
setup.dealing: The 32 tiles are shuffled face down. Each player receives 8 tiles, usually dealt in batches of 4 (wood stacks).

rules.objective: Score points by winning the final trick of each round and by capturing 'special' high-ranking tricks.
rules.gameplay: 1. **Opening**: The dealer (East) leads the first trick. 2. **Leading**: A player can lead a single tile, a pair (e.g., Heaven Pair), a triple, or a quad. 3. **Following**: Others must play the same number of tiles. To win, tiles must be higher in rank and of the same suit (Civil/Military). If a player cannot beat the lead, they discard tiles face down. 4. **Suits**: The tiles are divided into 22 'Civil' tiles (11 pairs) and 10 'Military' tiles. Civil leads must be beaten by Civil; Military by Military. 5. **Final Trick**: The winner of the 8th (final) trick becomes the dealer for the next round and scores points. Winning the final trick is the primary goal.
keyRules: Only the winner of a trick can lead the next trick.
Civil pairs (e.g., 6-6 and 6-6) can only be beaten by higher-ranking Civil pairs.
Mixed sets (Civil + Military) have specific complex ranking rules.
If you win the 8th trick after winning no other tricks, you 'Small Win'.
Winning the 8th trick having won all previous tricks is 'Great Win' (very rare).

strategy.basic: Conserve your highest-ranking pairs (like the Heaven or Earth pairs) for the later tricks. The game is won or lost on the final tile.
strategy.intermediate: Watch the discards carefully to determine which Military tiles (the 'singles') are still in play. Since there is only one of each Military tile rank, knowing what has fallen is critical to knowing if your tile is the current 'boss'.
strategy.advanced: Master the 'Supreme Pair' (Gee Joon) logic. The 1-2 and 2-4 tiles are the weakest individually but the strongest together as a pair. Using them correctly to break up an opponent's high pair lead is the mark of an expert.
tips: Never lead a high Civil tile if you don't have its pair; it will likely be captured.
Use your low 'trash' tiles for discards when you cannot win a trick.
Try to keep track of the number of tiles remaining in the Civil vs. Military suits.

difficulty.easy: Plays highest tile whenever possible; discards high tiles by mistake.
difficulty.medium: Tracks highest remaining tiles; saves high pairs for the last three tricks; understands Civil/Military suit distinction.
difficulty.hard: Full card counting (tile tracking); calculates probabilities of opponents holding specific pairs; subtle 'Gee Joon' strategy for breaking leads.

considerations: The AI must manage 32 unique tiles across two distinct suits (Civil/Military).
Tactical evaluation should prioritize the 8th trick over earlier tricks.
Must handle complex 'Mixed Set' ranking logic for pairs and triples.

engine.deckDescription: A Chinese domino deck consisting of 32 tiles organized into specialized suits representing traditional Chinese domino combinations, commonly used in Chinese tile games as an alternative to standard Western playing cards.
engine.suitDescription: Chinese domino tiles organized by traditional suit categories based on domino pips (dot patterns), where the specific arrangements and suits reflect the hierarchical structure of Chinese domino gaming traditions.
engine.rankDescription: Domino tiles ranked by their pip combinations, where specific tiles and their doubles have traditional names and values in Chinese games, determining card strength and strategic importance during gameplay.

hero.title: TIEN GOW
hero.subtitle: The Heaven Nine Game
hero.tagline: Master the oldest tile-taking game in history. Win the final trick, win the game.

synthesis.shortDescription: The supreme trick-taking game of Ancient China, played with a ritualistic set of 32 dominoes. Strategy lies in the Civil and Military suits.

prompts.human: Welcome to Tien Gow. You have 8 tiles. Use your Civil pairs and Military singles to capture tricks. Remember, the 8th trick is the one that truly counts!
prompts.ai: Game: Tien Gow (Chinese Dominoes). 32 tiles, 4 players. Trick-taking mechanics with Civil/Military suit restrictions. Key objective: Win the 8th trick. Special ranking for Gee Joon pair (1-2, 2-4).

scoring.description: Points are awarded to the winner of the 8th trick. Bonuses for capture of high-ranking pairs or triplets.
scoring.winCondition: Highest point total after 4 rounds (North, East, South, West) wins.

nullReasons.targetScore: No fixed target score; play by game rules.
